title: The Browser Rendering Pipeline
summary: The browser turns HTML and CSS into layout, paint, layers, and visible pixels.

subtopics.title: HTML parsing
subtopics.explanation: The browser reads HTML and builds a tree of elements called the DOM. Malformed markup may still render, but the browser can repair it unexpectedly. It is like turning a written outline into a tree of rooms. Semantic elements help browsers and assistive technology understand the structure. For example, a missing closing tag can change the DOM tree the browser constructs. For example, inspect the DOM tree when the browser repairs malformed nesting.

subtopics.title: CSS matching
subtopics.explanation: The browser reads CSS and decides which styles apply to each element. It builds style information for the page. It is like choosing the right paint and measurements for each room. Complex selectors and large stylesheets can add work, but measure before assuming they are the bottleneck. For example, a broad CSS selector may match many nodes, but measure before treating it as slow. For example, use computed styles to find the rule that produced the current appearance.

subtopics.title: Layout
subtopics.explanation: Layout calculates where boxes appear and how large they are. Changing width or font size can move nearby content. It is like rearranging furniture and finding that the walkway changed. Reserve image dimensions and avoid unnecessary layout changes to reduce visible jumps. For example, a newly loaded font can change line breaks and move content below it. For example, reserve image space to prevent text moving when the asset arrives.

subtopics.title: Paint and composite
subtopics.explanation: Painting turns text, colors, borders, and images into drawing work; compositing combines layers into the final frame. It is like painting separate scenery and combining it into one stage view. Some transform and opacity animations can avoid repeated layout, but profile the actual interaction. For example, a transform animation may avoid recalculating layout for every frame. For example, measure a frame before changing an animation property for performance.

subtopics.title: JavaScript and interaction
subtopics.explanation: JavaScript can change content and styles, which may require the browser to repeat some work. Long tasks can delay interaction. It is like pausing stage preparation to rewrite the set while the audience waits. Break up expensive work and measure real user timing. For example, a long click handler can make a visible button feel unresponsive. For example, break up a long handler when interaction becomes delayed.

foundations.overview: The browser rendering pipeline turns HTML, CSS, images, and JavaScript into visible pixels and interactive controls. It builds a document tree, matches styles, calculates positions, paints, and combines layers. Think of it like reading a plan, arranging objects, then painting a scene. Knowing these steps helps explain layout shifts and slow pages, but measure before optimizing.
foundations.whyItMatters: The pipeline is a mental model for finding where visible work happens. Use profiling to confirm which stage is expensive before changing the implementation.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser builds the DOM and style information, calculates layout, paints, and composites frames. Rendering tools help connect code changes to this work.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Use performance panels to see whether parsing, scripting, layout, painting, or network time dominates a slow page.
foundations.businessImpact: Stable layouts and responsive controls help people finish tasks without waiting or losing their place.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Optimize the measured bottleneck; avoid assuming every style or script causes a slow page.
foundations.performanceImpact: Reduce render-blocking resources, long JavaScript tasks, and layout shifts.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The browser always paints only once
commonMisconceptions.reality: Changes, interactions, and arriving assets can trigger additional layout and paint work.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A smaller bundle guarantees a fast page
commonMisconceptions.reality: Network size matters, but execution, layout, and rendering can also be the bottleneck.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The browser completes each rendering stage only once.
commonMisconceptions.reality: DOM, style, and layout changes can trigger later work again during interaction.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A transform is always faster than every other animation.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The benefit depends on the page and device; profile the actual animation and avoid excess layers.

keyTakeaways: The browser reads HTML and builds a tree of elements called the DOM.
The browser reads CSS and decides which styles apply to each element.
Layout calculates where boxes appear and how large they are.
Painting turns text, colors, borders, and images into drawing work; compositing combines layers into the final frame.
JavaScript can change content and styles, which may require the browser to repeat some work.
